opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think 2025 is going to be a year where a lot of people are surprised, in both directions.

On one side, there's been a narrative that pre-training is hitting a wall. Scaling pre-training does get harder. You need more compute, more data, bigger clusters, and each step takes longer to come together. So you might not see the same dramatic jump from one generation of base model to the next on the timeline people have gotten used to.

But I think that misses what's actually happening. The big story is reasoning, test-time compute. With models like o1 we've opened a new scaling axis. Instead of only making the model bigger, you let it think longer and train it with reinforcement learning to think well. That axis is very early. It's much cheaper to make progress there right now than on pre-training, so I'd expect really rapid capability gains in 2025, especially in domains where you can check the answer: math, coding, some areas of science.

The third piece is agents. Reasoning is what makes agents feasible. To do a long task, take actions in the world, use a computer, and recover from mistakes, you need a model that can plan and correct itself over many steps. I think 2025 is the year we start seeing agents that actually work for real, if fairly narrow, tasks. They won't be perfectly reliable. Reliability is the hard part, and going from 90% to 99% to 99.9% is where a lot of the work is. But it'll start to feel real.

So my summary is that progress is going to look less like one giant leap from a bigger model and more like steady, compounding improvements from reasoning and RL, which turn into products that can actually do work for you. If you only watch the pre-training headlines, you might think things are slowing down. I think it's going to be quite the opposite.

r001.rationale: The response calls reasoning and test-time compute “the big story” and says they will drive rapid capability gains in 2025.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that 2025 is going to be the year where people realize that pre-training is no longer the only game in town, and that the progress is going to come from stacking a few different things on top of each other.

The first is reasoning. What we saw with o1 is that if you let the model think before it answers, and you train it with reinforcement learning to think well, you get a very different kind of capability jump than you get from just making the base model bigger. And the important thing about that is it's a new axis to scale on. You can scale the amount of compute at training time, but you can also scale the amount of compute the model spends at test time, and those compound. So I'd expect the reasoning models to get a lot better over the course of the year, and to get better in ways that feel a little jagged, where they're superhuman at some math or coding problem and then still a bit clumsy at something that seems much easier.

The second thing is that pre-training keeps going. It's slower, it's more expensive, the gains per dollar are smaller than they were, but the bigger models are still better, and people shouldn't write that off. It's just that it's no longer the whole story.

And then the third piece, which I think is actually the one that matters most for how people experience 2025, is agents. The models are now good enough at reasoning that you can start handing them multi-step tasks, let them use tools, let them take actions in a browser or in a codebase, and have them actually complete the thing rather than just suggest the next step. That's the shift from "the model is a smart assistant that answers my question" to "the model goes and does something for me while I'm not watching." I think coding is where that shows up first, because the feedback loops are clean and you can verify the output. But you'll start to see it in more open-ended computer use too.

So if I had to put it in one sentence, I'd say 2025 is less about one big new model and more about the combination of reasoning plus test-time compute plus tool use starting to produce things that feel genuinely agentic. And I think the reliability curve on those agents is the thing to watch, because a demo that works eighty percent of the time is interesting and a system that works ninety-nine percent of the time changes how you work.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial improvement in reasoning, but describes 2025 progress as a combination of reasoning, continued pre-training, and agents. It says agents matter most for how people experience the year, so it does not clearly identify reasoning as the defining focus of AI capability progress.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see progress along two dimensions. One is making the models more capable: better at reasoning through difficult problems, writing code, and handling tasks that take multiple steps. The other is turning those capabilities into something people can actually use reliably.

For 2025, I’m particularly interested in models that can spend more time thinking about a problem before answering. That gives us another way to improve performance, beyond just training a bigger model. But the question is how consistently that translates into useful work.

I expect we’ll see more systems that can take a task, work on it for a while, check their results, and come back to you when they need help. I think that progress will be uneven. A model might do something remarkably sophisticated and then stumble on something that seems simple. So I’d watch how much work you can successfully delegate, and how much supervision it still requires.

r001.rationale: The response highlights reasoning and models spending more time thinking, but presents these as one part of progress alongside practical reliability and delegation. It does not predict reasoning will be the defining focus of AI progress in 2025.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect we’ll see progress on two fronts. Models will keep getting better through training, but we’ll also get more capability by giving them more time to reason through a problem before answering. That’s particularly useful for things like coding and math, where you can check whether an answer actually works.

The other big development will be turning those capabilities into systems that can carry out longer tasks. It’s one thing to answer a question well; it’s another to work through a sequence of steps, notice a mistake, and recover. I think we’ll see meaningful progress there in 2025, though reliability will still be a major constraint. The interesting question will be how much useful work a system can finish without someone having to intervene.

r001.rationale: The response predicts gains from more reasoning time, but presents this as one of two fronts alongside longer-task systems. It does not identify reasoning as the defining focus of 2025 progress.
